analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal land grazing rules to give ranchers longer, transferable permits and a new fee formula.
analysis.headline: The bill won 18 cosponsors and a favorable committee report in July 1995, but it sat on the Senate calendar and never came to a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how livestock grazing is run on federal land across the West. It would give ranchers 15-year permits with first priority for renewal, make their grazing preference a transferable right attached to their private "base property," and replace the existing fee formula with one based on the gross value of livestock production. It would also pull National Grasslands out of the National Forest System, limit environmental review of grazing permits, and bar anyone but government staff or consultants hired by ranchers from monitoring range conditions.
analysis.who_benefits: Western ranchers who hold federal grazing permits. They would gain longer, more secure permits, transferable grazing rights that add market value to their ranches, a new fee formula set by livestock production rather than the old statutory formula, the right to pledge permits as loan collateral with guaranteed renewal, protection from additional environmental review, and freedom from monitoring by outside parties. Banks and agricultural lenders also gain, because permits pledged for loans would carry guaranteed renewal for up to 15 years.

how_it_helps.text: Grazing permits and leases would run 15 years, and the current holder would get first priority for renewal if the land stays open and they comply with the terms.
A rancher's grazing preference would attach to their private base property and could be transferred with a sale, making the federal grazing right a form of property that adds value to the ranch.
The existing statutory grazing fee formula would be repealed and replaced with a fee based on the three-year average gross value of beef production.
Permits could be pledged as security for ranch loans, and lenders would get a guaranteed renewal of pledged permits for up to 15 years.

Issuing a permit consistent with the land use plan would require no additional environmental study under the National Environmental Policy Act, and compliance monitoring would be limited to government personnel or consultants retained by the permittee or the United States.
If federal land were taken out of grazing for a public purpose, permittees would get two years' notice and compensation at fair market value for their permanent range improvements.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers, who own the land and would collect whatever the new fee formula produces in place of the existing one — the bill itself directs annual reports on grazing revenues and costs. Other users of the public rangelands — hunters, anglers, and wildlife watchers — would bear reduced flexibility, since grazing levels could not fall below those authorized as of August 1, 1993 and reductions over 10 percent would be phased in over five years.

drawbacks.text: The bill states that nothing in it may reduce the levels of livestock grazing authorized as of August 1, 1993, locking in stocking levels regardless of later range conditions.
Any change in grazing use exceeding 10 percent would be phased in over five years, slowing action on land that monitoring shows is being overgrazed.
Compliance monitoring would be limited to the government and consultants retained by permittees themselves, excluding independent observers from documenting range damage.
Issuing a grazing permit consistent with a land use plan would trigger no additional environmental analysis under NEPA, removing a check on individual permit decisions.
National Grasslands would be removed from the National Forest System and managed under a program oriented to livestock grazing purposes.

The bill repeals the 1978 rangeland law's findings and fee formula and would entitle permittees to compensation whenever permits are canceled for a public purpose, creating a federal liability for future land decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For permit holders the gains are large and concrete: longer security, transferable rights, loan collateral, and a fee formula of their choosing. The costs fall on the public side of the ledger — grazing effectively frozen at 1993 levels, slow five-year phase-ins for reductions, monitoring restricted to friendly parties, and environmental review pared back. The bill does contain real conservation tools, including suspension of grazing for drought or fire and limits tied to the land's livestock carrying capacity, but its own rule that nothing shall reduce 1993 grazing levels undercuts them.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Energy Committee approved and reported the bill in late July 1995 and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but it was never brought up for a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Domenici introduced the bill on May 25, 1995 with 17 co-introducers, including Majority Leader Bob Dole and three Democrats (Conrad, Dorgan, and Baucus).
The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee held hearings on June 22, 1995.

On July 28, 1995 the committee reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment, Senate Report 104-123; committee Democrats filed minority views, and the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 158.
No floor vote ever followed; the bill died on the calendar when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public kept the existing grazing system, including environmental review of permits and the executive-branch rangeland reforms of that era; western ranchers did not obtain the longer transferable permits, the new fee formula, or the monitoring restrictions the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept existing grazing rules

for.name: Sen. Pete Domenici
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 17 co-introducers from both parties.

for.name: Sen. Frank Murkowski
for.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: 15 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Craig, Hatch, Burns, Dole, and Gramm.

for.name: 3 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill from plains and mountain states with large grazing interests.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Democrats
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views opposing the bill when it was reported on July 28, 1995.

against.name: Clinton administration (Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the legislation while implementing its own rangeland management reforms for the Bureau of Land Management.

against.name: Conservation and wildlife groups
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the 1995 Senate grazing bill, objecting to frozen grazing levels and weakened environmental oversight.

sides.party_line_note: Support was 15 Republicans joined by 3 Democrats from grazing states, and committee Democrats filed minority views when the bill was reported.

industries.industry: Western livestock ranchers (federal grazing permit holders)
industries.note: The bill would lock in and expand ranchers' access to public land: 15-year transferable preferences with priority renewal, a fee formula based on livestock production value, and grazing levels that could not drop below 1993 authorizations. Their gain comes at the cost of public flexibility to reduce grazing on damaged land and of whatever return taxpayers would otherwise get.

Grazing permits could be pledged as security for ranch loans, with guaranteed renewal up to 15 years, making federal grazing rights dependable loan collateral. The effect on the public is indirect, flowing through western farm credit.
